items.body:
The jittery pulses and waking dream-like atmospheres of Dx2ov land on London’s Blank Mind for an album strafing between cut-up sound poetry and whisked garage-house.

“Dx2ov arrives on Blank Mind with Tonegues, his second vinyl LP following on from Interzona on Gost Zvuk in 2024. The LP title is a wordplay on the idea of speaking in tongues and sonic tonalities, echoing the process and dialogue that went into creating the record. Taken from a vast archive of material from 2019-2025, these ideas were arranged with the collaboration of label owner Sam Purcell and then completed with the long-distance assistance of Toupaz.

Tonegues is best seen through the lens of a beat-tape, with the playful flow and variety that the format provides, bursting with oddball ideas and punctuated with intangible vocal samples. Much like the LP’s beguiling, hand-drawn artwork by Wolfgang Matuschek, it is a glimpse into an inner world, a portal to somewhere uncanny and strange borne through imagination.

Light dub flourishes mix with footwork/IDM hybrids and understated, melancholic synthesis on ‘2018’, whilst the loose, rhythmic march of ‘Fon32’ evokes the dusty beatdown styles of early 2000s Detroit downtempo records. Whilst on one of the LP highlights ‘Trout’ he lays down a gleefully strange bed for the surrealist storytelling of Jacob Dwyer about interactions with dogs, dripping old houses and a perennial wish for the phone to ring with a heavy dub poetry slant. Dx2ov swiftly moves through more footwork adjacent, almost bedroom hyper-pop territories with a penchant for gabber kicks on ‘No Strings (feat DJ Paprika)’ and the maximalism of album closer 'Demetch' which continues in the tradition of wonky, mid-2010s UK bass music flips. The outcome is a confounding, unorthodox piece of work, zigzagging between forms, textures and moods.”

items.body:
Sickest no-wave machine sputter by debut duo Murray Collier (Grim Lusk, Dip Friso) & Conal Blake (Feedback Moves, Domestic Exile) aka Inweys, sliced and spiced like a deep fried Haswell meets Foodman vibes, recorded in the summer of 2024 at La Chunky Studios in Glasgow

“Inweys debut release arrives as four pieces of broken body music. Lurking, barely human fragments brought into the present. Using a short drum-machine improvisation as core material, the pieces are formed from a processes of mining and re-mining for small details, with each fragment zoomed in on and turned into new pieces. There’s a transformation taking place, but one that doesn’t obscure the materiality of the recording tapes as sticky, corrosive matter. On skewed and stretched fabric they enact their palimpsestic play, sketching and altering the grid with itchy technologies. What their edits and improvisations don’t say they let space say the rest, with vacuum aerated frames for bass to diffuse and beats to wriggle. More King Tubby than Cage, more Mantronix than Reich: minimalism with molten tips.

Both Conal and Murray’s past work has embraced malleable and iterative technologies; music whose feeliness figures itself out in space in a messy precomposed/improvised dialectic. This is the sort of thing most “new music” experimentalists (or anyone who spends most of their time obsessively manipulating tapes in expensive studios) often can’t achieve; a liveness, birthed from learning in situated play. Like the lore of Phuture’s Acid Trax, a poverty of material is at the heart of this, rendering the work with an abortive conviction: a corpse waking to consciousness becomes amphibious. Instead of the composer we have a relation, two people navigating the awkward spooling between the two reels of tape. Inweys is scots for “inwards”, and in their working process this is what they do. But the result is circular motion. Until the tape runs out, all in ways move out”. "

Fielding Hope.

items.body:
Alex Zhang Hungtai pivots yet again on 'Orion/Mother', playing (mostly) trumpet alongside some of the New York City underground scene's most intriguing improvisers, including Kwami Winfield, Laura Cocks, Lester St. Louis, TAK Ensemble's Madison Greenstone, 75 Dollar Bill's Che Chen and Leo Chang.

 'Orion/Mother' has its roots in a set of home recordings Zhang made with some of his talented local friends; "playing with you all deeply informed my current understanding in improvisation," he explains in his thank you note, "without you this album would not have existed." So over a two week period, in a rehearsal space in New York, he invited a handful of his friends to start "an ad-hoc group", playing trumpet over chopped up home recordings and wrenching them into the future. And while the finished article - split into two distinct sections - is long, it's fully worthy of your attention. As always, Zhang brings a unique ear into the room, resisting any usual improv tropes to concentrate on sounds that most artists would avoid - unruly resonances, glitches, off-piste rhythms and unsubtle interferences.

At it's best, the record sounds like jazz specters vanishing thru faded noise remnants and the wreckage of lost experiments. On 'Shadow Integration', Zhang's brassy wails echo out over a slippery, semi-rhythmic drum machine pattern, and on 'Tanhäuser Gate', the trumpet is even more isolated, weeping over a muted soundscape that's credited simply as "Ableton" on the accompanying notes. He maintains the same energy when he's working side-by-side with his collaborators, too, finding space for Winfield's circuit bent belches on 'Nataraja' and Chen and Chang's percussion on the jaw-droppingly spannered opener 'Sidewinder'. And even when the tone shifts on 'Mother', heading into a lighter (comparatively at least) zone on the woodwind-heavy 'Kali', Zhang has a knack for tying everything together with his lyrical performance. Just peep the title track, almost seven minutes of uncanny clanks and Tōru Takemitsu-strength murmurs that Zhang butters with pure improvised emotion.

items.body:
Potent, lysergic lounge music and psych-fonk-exotica out of Brussels, with Michael Crabbé letting everything slosh out of the lines in a real slow burn head melter, like Spencer Clark meets Giulio Erasmus and Pekka Airaksinen on some vintage Hoffmans. Another wyrd doozy from Antwerp’s reliably off-the-wall label, Souvenirs From Imaginary Cities.

“Straight from the weedy fields of swampville Bruxelles we bring you 8 ‘tranches de vie’ of deep zone-hall by weirdtronic bass veteran Michael Crabbé’s best fitting sound costume to date: the mighty Rudi J! You might know him from earlier outfits but that’s not the main issue here. Rudi J is!

When this swamp thing touches the pads, it’s off-road after three seconds, even if you’re in the middle of Europe’s capital. Mixing analog dirt and digital sound bits in a very loose and personal take on dancehall, we’re pretty far away from the dance floor but definitely swinging. It’s a trippy affair wandering around concrete flowers with a deep ambient flavor, but it’s edgy.

A hot summer fever dream following his own lusty path, full of life and wonder but with something sinister hiding around every corner. Often reaching for the stars, a deeper shade of bass keeps things nicely grounded. These sounds are built with a sound system in mind and bass culture at heart. Even if you can definitely surf on it from your couch, picking out all of its ear-pricking details, it will very much come alive on a big sound.

A layered affair with almost jazzy and orchestral elements peeping through the stereo-field, spectral and dissonant but also playful. Like early dubstep, some of these tunes can destroy a clubsound, keeping you skunking out in pedestrian mode and snorting up the atmospherics, finally forgetting about that damn phone.”

items.body:
London/Helsinki label Cold Blow map the subliminal links of early ‘90s electro, techno and its backroom, downbeat offshoots thru a plethora of tunes recorded ’92-’99 by the likes of Stasis, 2000 And One, CiM, all displaying how they translated Detroit techno intricacies and new age ambient soul for UK & EU bodies in motion, or those eaten by sofas.

“Across eight carefully selected slices of starry-eyed machine soul, Cold Blow presents an exquisite tour through backroom techno and downtempo electro. With a focus on thematic flow and an immersive listening experience, the London-based label explores works from leading lights of the 1990s and previously unreleased cuts that celebrate the human heart that can be discovered in synthetic sound practices.

The development of techno in the 1990s saw the music evolve in different directions across the world. From the expressive blueprint laid out by the Detroit pioneers, a wide range of tempos and energies emerged. Techno's evocative synthesis and intricate drum machine programming was especially potent for deeper explorations away from the dancefloor.

Documents Of Different Reality casts back to when technology was steering quantum leaps in communication and creativity and the future was shot through with naive optimism. It was also a time when the media and industry hadn't caught up with the music to box it into distinct categories. As such, there's a sense of creative freedom that informs the older tracks on the album, from 2000 And One and Sandy Huner's (originally as Pure) sparkling example of early Dutch techno to London-based LA Synthesis' detailed take on braindance and the majestic night sky vision of cult legend Stasis.

There's also space for rare, late 90s machine funk from Icelandic outlier Thor alongside Connective Zone's charmingly fractured bleep dream and a more contemporary offering from Barcelona-based duo Permutation. Meanwhile Mind Control and CiM both capture the spirit of stylistic fusion with twitchier rhythms that take influence from hardcore and jungle as much as techno.

With an atmospheric through-line of melancholic pads and harmonious leads, this small but perfectly formed collection naturally follows on from previous, equally thought-out compilations on Cold Blow, and adds a distinct perspective on the history and continuing legacy of pioneering early ambient techno.”

Back by demand - 2nd hand copies are known to trade for triple figures - Cindy’s timeless suite of sexy, hazed dream-pop is acutely tipped to anyone who holds a flame for Julee Cruise, Voice Actor, Lynch, Enya, Bianca Scout, Vince Clarke...

‘I’m Cindy’ is a chef’s kiss of effortlessly slow, seductive lo-fi songwriting that practically smushes earlobes with its heavenly marriage of Kai Hugo's faded production lustre and singer, Blue LoLãn’s range of whispered sweet nothings and harmonised coos. In the years since its original release it’s taken on a life of its own as a go-to succour for lovers of blissed-out, cinematic waft with equal measures of soft-focus, nostalgic FM synths and details that caress and crack in all the right, tender places. 

Conceptually derived from Palmbomen II’s ‘Memories of Cindy’ session of 2017, the 13 tracks find marbled whorls of sensual fascination within that LP’s fantasy reminiscence, here expanded into a spectrum of LA-via-Antwerp dream-pop like Johnny Jewel meets Alex Zhang Hungtai on the synth and sax pearl ‘Another’ or lip-smacking cruiser ‘Justin’, thru a Voice Actor-esque ‘Voice Message’ and the gossamer FM synth fronds that wrap it up on ‘Maybe Because It’s Over Now’, whilst secreting shimmers of Vince Clarke ballads in ‘2y & 6m’, and acid-laced lo-fi machine crack shades away from Maria Minerva on ’Never Let Me Go’.

No brainer!

items.body:
Softly softly does it for the gorgeous debut duo of soundtrack composer Elori Saxl & saxophonist Henry Solomon with their lushly ephemeral grasp of 4th world ambient jazz, tipped for the anyone on the line between Lynch/Badalamenti, TLF Trio, Laurel Halo, Arve Henriksen or Alex Zhang-Hungtai's Love Theme side-wind.

Captured over a few days in LA, ‘Seeing Is Believing’ frames the sax player’s searching feel for tone across soundscapes sparingly coloured in subtle harmonic gradients by Elori Saxl’s fluttering Juno 106 keys. The nine parts are testament to the duo’s near-telepathic level of intuition and mutual vision of a palpably tissue-soft atmospheric music; one where spectres of ’70s minimalism and ’80s new age bleed forward into structures equally informed by soundsystem culture and contemporary pop production, achieving a sort of slow shifting, ecological pressure system that is a pleasure to sink into.

Within her richly visual, implicitly storytelling style, Elori Saxl draws on a wellspring of experience in composing for new music ensembles, and soundtracking and directing films for New Yorker and Slate, to set spacious dimensions for Solomon’s ruminative baritone sax and bass clarinet to wander freely. A quiet sense of restraint defines proceedings as their forms gently grow and sway from the dusky licks of ‘Reverence’ thru the gauzy lustre of the title piece, conjuring a geosmin waft in ‘Raindrops’ and LA hills panorama on ‘Reno Silver’, or balmiest breeze of Glass-like phrasing on ‘A Thousand Steps’, into the gorgeous, pitch bent and sensual sorcery summoned in standout ‘Heart.’

Stunner.

items.body:
Real heart-stopping, life-affirming, almost indescribably beautiful posthumous album featuring (for the first time) vocal works by beloved, dearly departed, Ethiopian nun and now-legendary pianist/composer Emahoy Tsege Mariam Gebru, room recorded straight to tape between 1977-1985, sounds of life just about audible in the background. Almost had an out of body experience listening to it the other night - just a perfect, 10/10 album.

’Souvenirs’ is an intimate self-portrait written, recorded and compiled by the late Emahoy Tsege Mariam Gebru; a classically-trained pianist turned nun, whose singular style of jazz and blues-inflected composition and performance became globally renowned in her latter years via reissues and compilations reaching as far back as the 1960s, namely the ‘Éthiopiques 21: Piano Solo’ CD and a much-prized eponymous set in 2016. At the age of 99, Emahoy passed away in Jerusalem last year, whilst planning towards this first ever showcase of her vocals - which have never appeared on her purely piano-based recordings until now, making for a truly life-affirming experience from its opening bars. 

The posthumous release, realised in collaboration with Emahoy’s family and Mississippi Records - is a stone cold stunner. It grants unprecedented access to her discrete craft and inner world in Addis Ababa, against a backdrop of the Ethiopian Red Terror and Civil War, prior to her subsequent exile in a Jerusalem convent. Whilst all no doubt defined by her signature, intricate and lilting type of classical meets jazz-blues phrasing, the eight songs are all far more concise than her usual instrumental works, made even more spellbinding by the revelation of her softly contoured and captivating vocals that beautifully trace and overlie the cadence of her keys. It’s just pure, unbridled expression that’s only heightened by the seemingly off-the-cuff nature of the recordings, as if she just sung the songs to herself, impromptu, never intended for public consumption.

Replete with incidental creaks of the piano stool, birds outside the window, and Emahoy’s finger on the record button, the songs depict themes of loss, mourning and soon-to-be exile, sung into a basic boombox. They place us in the room with her, closer than ever, privy to a vocal version of the closing number to her eponymous compilation, now unveiled as a dedication her niece, the titular Tenkou, with lyrics to guide her adulthood “Don’t cry / Childhood won’t come back / Let it go with love”, alongside the beatific, open-window paean ‘Clouds Moving on the Sky’, and melancholic hiraeth of ‘Ethiopia My Homeland’ or ‘Don’t Forget Your Country’, and ineffable, humbling elegance of idea and execution to ‘Is It Sunny or Cloudy in the Land You Live?’ and ‘Where is the Highway of Thought?’.

Unmissable.

items.body:
Gulp Joachim Nordwall’s queasiest, most curdled synth tones on this supremely detuned co-op with Athens’ Stellage crew = 45 minutes of pure nasal-drip tang and gungy pulses tipped FFO Connor Camburn, Wolf Eyes, Conrad Schnitzler, Ilpo Väisänen’s Liima alltimers.

Joachim Nordwall’s 1st solo jaunt since capping the ‘Healing Music’ series in ’23 finds the DIY linchpin and serial collaborator coaxing potently psychoactive tones from an undisclosed set up. It appears to be one of his most intently focussed jags in recent memory, concentrated on juicing a paucity of ingredients for optimal flavour. Nothing that new then? Well, aye, but when he really gets into it, with an effect that really probes parts of the psyche untouched by anything we’ve heard from him before, he produces synaesthetic sounds that frankly makes our ears salivate. 

A starting exercise in plucky pulse-work recalling Robert Aiki Aubrey Lowe initiates a real descent into the nether regions of Nordwall’s imagination, pulling into sepulchral drone on ‘Trance Recording’ and Droog wet dream material on ‘Abandoned Test Site’, while allowing for some levity in the lacquer-crackling pulse poem ‘Expand Your Mind’. However, he soon pitches back into resonant, metallic sonorities with durational conviction on a ‘Some Skies Overlap’ bringing to mind Connor Camburn works, but with an icier edge, and his title track spews molten drums in a rumbling, spark-spitting torrent. 

Proper filth. Snorkel it!

¿DONDEDOS, Pascual Martinez and Jeremy Castillo, release Drifting Nowhere via Rubadub

"¿DONDEDOS is young dude/unc duo hailing from the Mission. Pascual Martinez (young dude) and BPT head honcho Jeremy Castillo (unc) have spent the last few years in the stu, cooking up this deep fried, groovin' 4 tracker. Fans of 2011-16 LIES and Future Times releases, “Biology" era Young Marco, Juju and Jordash, and the Wah Wah Wino crew are in for a treat.

In an era where literally every aspect of dance music is overly programmed and manicured, ¿DONDEDOS take a massively refreshing approach marked by true experimentation. All drums were recorded on the Roland R8, and the melodies were live played with a loose, jammy feel not felt on many electronic 12" releases in 2026. They're a jam band baby!!!!! 

The fun starts with "Drifting Nowhere," a fried oddball deep house record with one of the year's most infectious basslines. Be ready for it to be on a loop in your brain long after the track has stopped playing.

2nd track "Dies Varos" was described by BPT fam Izaak from Loveshadow as sounding like "part of the Mediterranean touching Mexico." Ahhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh. (that was a deep relaxed sigh, not a scream for once!!!)

"Music for Patios" sounded pretty good on a walk and not on a patio so, just FYI, only a suggestion not a requirement. 

Ender Noche Caminando features Diego Herrera (AKA Suzanne Kraft) on sax. In Jeremy's own words, this track features "oddball dancehall drums on the R8 with 80s synth pop dub melodic sensibilities." "

items.body:
More gold from Japan’s endlessly curious Em Records, this time shining a light on southern Californian post-minimalist composer Jeff Bruner, highlighted by Visible Cloaks’ Spencer Doran and bringing together stunning works spanning 1978 - 2020 for mbira, calypso dub and fretless gut-string banjo - huge tip FFO Richard Crandell, Terry Riley, Roland P. Young, Takoma, General Strike, Daniel Lentz.

"I first came across Jeff's mysterious "Reggae Foes" 45 in the mid-2000s at the legendary Logos book/record store in Santa Cruz, California (RIP) - the kind of generic sleeve and label that gives you nothing more than a font and some scant shards of text to go by (luckily this text was "A Flying Saucer Came Down and Burnt My Baby's Neck"). What I heard upon bringing it home felt like some kind of alternate-timeline post punk calypso, unknowingly adjacent to the deconstructions occurring at the Black Ark or in David Cunningham's early productions. When I finally talked to Jeff many years later, I was even more surprised to learn that he was also entrenched in southern California's post-minimalist composer scene in the 1970s alongside many of my compositional heroes, work which this compilation presents for the first time. Couldn't think of a better place for it to be transmitted from than EM!" (Spencer Doran/Visible Cloaks)

Four Corners is a compilation that showcases the various facets of American West Coast minimalist composer Jeff Bruner, with pieces from the 1970s to the 2020s displaying a cohesive set of aesthetic concerns. Bruner has a kinship with the composers Harold Budd and Daniel Lentz, the latter being a mentor to Bruner, and one can hear a relationship with the music of other minimal/post-minimal composers such as John Adams and Terry Riley. 1979's "Magic Mbira", a key piece in this collection, particularly highlights a Riley-esque element, and with its skillful use of tape delays reminiscent of Lenz's cascading echo system. Bruner and his mbira piece also have musical affinities with Roland P. Young and his classic Isophonic Boogie Woogie, in their shared melodic and structural concerns, as well as a desire to perform their compositions in a wider range of performance spaces, away from traditional recital halls. Another side of Bruner is revealed in the funhouse-mirror "Reggae Foes", a deconstructionist post-punk calypso-reggae tune and skewed Black Ark filtered through Cunningham/Toop's General Strike. The remaining two pieces are melancholy beauties of solo instrumentation: "Cold Rain and Snow" is a fretless gut-string banjo re-imagining of an American folk song; "Remembrance in a Pale Room" is a lovely piano piece dedicated to Lentz. Bruner has built upon a tradition, altering and adding to it with his individual vision, giving us this collection of intriguing and beautiful music. Available on CD/Vinyl/Digital, with E/J liner notes by Jeff Bruner, rare photos & the score for "Magic Mbira"."

items.body:
Memotone’s sublime, world-building ambient-jazz-fusion project yields a total gem for Accidental Meetings, perfused with the presence of Ugné Uma, Typesun & Jabu on a new highlight of his personalised microcosm, tipped for anyone on the line from Savath & Savalas to Moritz Von Oswald Trio, The Necks to Laurel Halo.

Active since 2011, it’s been a real pleasure to hear Will Yates cultivate his memotone sound into something more complex, yet not necessarily more complicated, on a slew of LPs for the likes of TTT, Sähkö, and World of Echo, plus that ace cut on Carrier’s debut LP. Club music is now long in the rearview, while ambient and jazz musics have taken precedence as the multi-instrumentalist continues to diversify his creative binds across more free-formed, expressive soundscapes, breezing with elements of spiritual jazz as much as psych folk, post rock,contemporary classical and strands of electronic music. 

‘Warm Shadows’ features some of his most seductive and expansive work, shaped with an underlying grasp of abstract, instrumental narratives that have become his calling card during this last decade. Intimacy and slowness are key to his exquisitely hushed appeal; unfolding the softest brushstrokes with patient electroacoustic nuance and attention to detail on two standouts with emergent Lithuanian vocalist Ugné Uma, who channels a mix of smouldering spiritual jazz and Eastern European melancholy on ‘Laimèti Pavyksta’, and even Sade-esque soul on the dusky closer ‘You Are Different.’ 

Elsewhere, the Bristolian connection makes for another highlight with Jabu’s Jasmine Butt’s subtle contribution to ‘Round The Bend,’ comparable to something from BoC’s ‘Campfire Headphase’, but left to his own devices memotone proves a consummate, atmospheric storyteller. Opener ‘For The Feral’ feels like a miniature of The Necks, and his feel for dreamy electro-acoustic texture best comes into play on ‘One Winged Bird’ and the tongue-tip moisture in the air of ‘The Freedom,’ all pointing to an artist arguably in their imperial phase. 

Tip!

items.body:
A digestibly pared-down version of Félicia Atkinson's 90-minute score to Georges Franju's controversial French horror film 'Les yeux sans visage' ('Eyes Without A Face'), 'SANS VISAGE' is her most sinister material to date, made on piano and keyboards and improvised to the film. 

Atkinson was just a teenager when she first saw Franju's 1960 film and it moved her enough that when she was approached by Belgian cultural institute VIERNULVIER to work on a new score, she knew exactly how to approach it. She remembered how impactful the film's themes had been and how resonant they were even decades later, where violence against women is still nauseatingly commonplace. In the film, an adaptation of an even more disturbing novel by Jean Redon, a plastic surgeon stalks and kills women who look like his disfigured daughter, removing their faces in an attempt to create a new one for her. Atkinson dedicates her slow-motion, menacing soundtrack to Gisèle Pelicot, remarking how patriarchal violence cycles again and again through history, creating cages within cages for women. But there's hope; Atkinson doesn't languish in darkness and terror, she knows that in there somewhere, liberation might be on the horizon. 

Underneath the grim, gloomy electric piano notes and agonising pauses, Atkinson seems to relish in a sense that escape might be possible. And if you've seen the film then you'll realise that she's acknowledging the fact that Dr. Génessier, the antagonistic surgeon, meets a fittingly grisly end. While he's let off the hook by police, his daughter Christiane is horrified by his crimes, freeing the dogs he was experimenting on and letting them take their revenge. It's a horror film, after all. But Aktinson swerves all the usual tropes; she improvises an impressionistic dream of wailing tones and aborted phrases that centre the resolution, not the torture itself. Re-scores are often a creative dead end, but thankfully this one adds texture, color and new context to the source material - it makes us want to watch the film all over again.

items.body:
New LP from French-born, London-based composer and musician Pascal Bideau via Tonal Union.

"Cartographers and US multinational technology corporations might think they’ve mapped out most of our big, beautiful blue planet, and yet there’s always more to discover if you know where to look. French-born, London-based composer and musician Pascal Bideau takes this as his central premise on a new album of intrepid sonic exploration that delights in the sensation of being somewhere you’ve never been before. ‘Terra Incognita’ invites us to seven faraway sonic imaginariums fusing global and spiritual jazz with life affirming minimalism into a hypnotic, polyrhythmic odyssey.

This time, the albums’ sound palette is more vibrant, earthy and abundant, drawing inspiration from the radiating optimism and high-energy sources heard in Afrobeat, Highlife and Electronic Afro-pop music, sounding looser, free and primarily interested in raw sensations. Antithetical to the precise ostinatos and gamelan patterns of the acclaimed debut ‘Fleeting Future’ (2022) and ‘Lines’ (2023). Terra Incognita, then, is a hybrid blend of traditional music and modern electronics, a trip into the unknown that ambulates freely, taking pleasure in its repetitions and never staying still. Bideau suggests this unmarked territory could be as much a fantasyland as it is a transportive journey into the inner self."

items.body:
Adrian Rew's properly hypnotic cult classic 'Slot Machine Music' has finally been reissued and it sounds even more terrifying and prescient than it did back in 2013 at the height of the basement noise era. One of the best environmental recording records bar none - don't sleep.

Back in 2009, PAN released its fourth album, 'Kenrimono', a set of recordings made by Greek sound artist Ilios at Japanese pachinko halls. The sheer density of it was as shocking and as intense as anything the noise genre had to offer, packed out with whirring, crunching and chiming resonances that took you to the smokey epicenter of the Japanese gambling world. And when 'Slot Machine Music' arrived a few short years later we assumed the sound would be similar; we were wrong. Initially dropped via Rew's own Ergot Records on CDr before the great Aaron Dilloway stepped in to handle the vinyl edition on his own Hanson imprint, the album seemingly grew from the Midwestern noise petri dish - but it wasn't an exercise in aesthetic posturing, using the racket of the modern American casino to mimic the intensity of a Wolf Eyes set. Instead, Rew was drawn to the experience itself, that's been meticulously designed by malign forces to guide behavior: those trapped inside the casino's four walls are seduced into spending more, losing more and returning to do it all over again.

Rew didn't know much about the environment when he visited Cleveland's Horseshoe Casino for the first time in 2013 armed with an Olympus LS-11 recorder and a camera. And over four months, he developed a peculiar relationship with the culture, surreptitiously taping the soundscapes at various Midwestern locations - in Michigan, Indiana, Ohio and Illinois - while attempting not to lose too much cash in the process. And it's a warts-n-all set, with dialog snippets and outdoor ambiance giving us more than simply the dense mass of chimes and stings and themes that you'd hear on the casino floor itself. What Rew is able to do is create a snapshot of a time and place, capturing the sheer desolation of the casino experience and using it to drive a narrative that Robert Altman would be proud of. The first thing you notice is that each machine's sounds are in tune with the next; "game designers," explains Rew, "tune their machines to the key of C in order to optimize harmonic cohesion." So although Rew's recordings are full-bodied, they're never too chaotic or discordant. 

Indeed, if you check in for the entire record - 2013's iconic 'Slot Machine Music' and its 2014 sequel 'Slot Machine Music Vol. 2' - you'll be lulled into the same false sense of security that entrances casino regulars. It's almost like ambient music, packed out with tiny sonic details that some well-paid sound engineer-cum-neurologist worked for years to figure out. Guided meditation music? New age crypto-psychedelia? It's all here, packaged in neon-lit one-armed-bandits aimed to target the dopamine centers of aging boomers with money to burn. And the best thing about the recordings is that Rew keeps some of the chatter intact, so we can hear him tangling with casino security, or haggling with his slot machine neighbors over change. We can hear the cheers and claps as paltry sums are won while vast fortunes are lost. The best moment for us comes when Rew wanders outside Grand Victoria Casino in Elgin, Illinois at the dead of night, the crickets singing as the machines echo from behind grand double doors. A freight train rushes past and blots out any other sound, distorting the recording.

It's a good reminder that although you might be able to hide from reality inside the casino, the Midwest will inevitably confront you with its rusted truth.

items.body:
Collaborative LP from Bristol mainstays Sam Binga & Addison Groove.

"Bristol's Sam Binga & Addison Groove have been friends and collaborators since their 2013 'BS3' EP, released on Modeselektor's '50 Weapons' imprint. This project, the third full-length on Binga’s Pineapple Records, is born from an intense 72-hour session at the legendary Devon Analogue Studios, where the pair were able to explore their mutual love of uptempo machine funk - whether that be Detroit Jit, Chicago Boxjams or Turbo Electro.

Three days of intense creativity across classic drum machines, vintage analogue synths and rare hardware effects resulted in a collection of raw but powerful audio building blocks - and over the past two years, the pair have been gradually shaping them into what is now a complete project - the BAGS INC album. Across 12 tracks, Binga & Addison explore that exciting space between 140 and 150 bpm - but while it's fast, it's not 'hard'; as you'd expect from the creators, it's still got that wiggle, and the all-important cheekiness for which they're known."

Heavy-lidded, late nite jazz-soul suss from the keenly touted Ugné Uma & producer emer, secreting a dozen sleepwalker specials on their duo debut with Stroom. FFO Leila, Lolina, ML Buch, Tirzah, Voice Actor.

Hashed out in imaginary air between Brussels and Berlin, ‘You and Me’ projects a mutual dream sequence of downbeat stardust and midnight jazz vapours supposed by two emergent figures of the EU undergrowth: one Ugné Uma paying up on the promise of her single for Somewhere Press, plus Marija Rasa’s emer, still fresh from a standout solo debut LP on Short Span in late ’25. In duo, they reaffirm, double down, and transcend the sum of their parts with a classy grasp of sandman tekkerz, suspending bodies between duvet-dive beatdown and hypnagogic soul with a slow-burn frisson of romantic intimacy.

With no hard edges or surprises for the supine mind, the album unfolds in its own liminal space with a gauzy sense of daydreamy-into-nocturnal physics. The filigree dub of emer’s ‘Fog’ LP is found dialled down to more powdery ambient jazz and soul smoulder, and inflected with a fine-wrought R&B discipline that ideally swirls Uma’s classic, smoky delivery, to the natural extent that it feels like they’ve been cooking together for years. Dusted but not dusty, it all treads the finest line of classic and modernist late nite needs for the ages, and especially hot, sleepless hours.

Sandwell District’s Dave Sumner aka Function completes his Existenz cycle for Tresor with an expansive, full spectrum strafe from beat-less ambient to slow acid, electro and signature deep techno gems.

Seven years since his ‘Existenz’ album for Tresor, and leading on from related EPs for Rrose’s Eaux and his own Infrastructure New York, Sumner reflects on what prompted his LP, and interim strife, across six tracks tallying to an LP in their own right. After immersion in his patented style of nocturnal pads and lustrous acid lines, it shouldn’t be hard to identify his touch on some of Sandwell District’s most romantic high points, finely-sculpted in a style that has served him damn well since the mid-late ‘90s origins of NYC & Brum techno.

Shine-eyed reflections of early ‘90s electronica radiate from opener ‘Ascent’ into 12 mins of sleekly heady, decelerated acid house less on ‘City of Luz’, and what could almost be an SD cut in the mouth-watering detailing and elegant drive of ‘Transmutation’. He continues to hanker for lushness in the club on the whirring, melancholic offbeat propulsion to another standout, ‘Growth Cycle (Hermetic Mix)’, before turning darker with flashes of Kraftwerk-via-his NYC electro touchstones on ‘November 29’, and deferred gratification of ‘Rubedo’.

Pavel Milyakov presents a third beautiful, bittersweet epitaph to his late foil, singer-songwriter Yana Pavlova - a Kyiv resident who passed at the tender age of 35 in 2025 - including her captivating covers of Tim Buckley and Spacemen 3.

Sharing its title with the final song issued during Yana Pavlova’s time, as found on the ‘Enthropic Vision’ (2024) 12”, and here in a subtly lighter version, ‘Thrill’ presents a definitive portrait of the artist’s quietly concentrated energies diffused across slowcore ambient shoegaze-pop soundscapes. Hailing to the same Kyiv underground scene that yielded Svitlana Nianio over 30 years ago, Pavlova’s music can be considered in a similar vein of strung-out Eastern European melancholy, and perhaps even more acutely with the revelation of Soloveyka’s Sade-esque soul stirrings on Stroom's comp of Ukrainian music. Comparisons aside, Pavlova's vocals possess a distinct pull all their own, and as Pavel Milyakov puts it: “full of true feeling, inner strength and melancholy."

The pair’s intuitive creative bond is palpable throughout ‘Thrill,’ where Milyakov underlines his spar with suitably stripped-down backdrops of drizzle, hazy strums and dusted downbeats to foreground Pavlova in the best, if fleeting, light. A fine strain of the atmospheric magick that coloured their ‘Blue’ and ‘Wandering’ albums of 2021 suffuses the 14 parts with a particular heartache, vacillating original compositions such as the folksy lament ‘strong-willed (rain version)’ and tongue-tip Ukrainian delivery of ‘nihil’ with exquisite sort of ambient-dub flip of ‘so hot (wash away all of my tears)’ that effectively brings Spacemen 3 closer to an imagined Rhythm & Sound x Sade. Elsewhere they saddle p hauntingly affective post-punk on ‘rise of music,’ and thee gauziest trip hop x shoegaze bliss-out ‘running through,’ plus a BoC-like interluud ‘never be the same,’ and supremely classy AOR soul drift in ‘healing sun 2.’ 

The final two tracks are a cold knockout, with the passage of her newly levitated (livicated) goth prayer ‘thrill,’ and closing cover of the Tim Buckley song (made famous by This Mortal Coil) ‘song to the siren’ assuring Pavlova’s quietly enduring legacy.

Abstract dub dream-weavers SKRS INTL. & WZRDRY remerge at the behest of Bristol’s Accidental Meetings for a super lush dose of wormholing ambient dance pressure tipped FFO Rezzett, Peak Oil/False Aralia, Second Woman.

‘Orbit Flares’ combines the two Canadian units for the first time in over a decade, naturally reprising an empathic level of vibes in a half hour of music that betrays illusive tekkerz developed over the interim. Any semblance of sharp edges are smudged to a brilliantly psychedelic, polychromatic lustre and laced with disciplined, yet properly wayward rhythms that tumble, buckle and vaporise in fractious delirium. Each new SKRS drop is welcome around ours but, jeez, they really push into their most impressive work here, possibly thanks to wzrdryAV’s synaesthetic suss.

Front to back it feel likes they catch minds/bodies in the split second before going under anaesthesia, and extrude us into pitch-bent helical vortices of plonging dub chords and gooey bass, finding bold new realms of computerised dub suss. Handrails are slippery as fuck, ground melts beneath feet, leaving bodies gyring in space between the weightless dub techno inflections of ‘1.1’, into air-stepping chicanery on ‘1.2’, or glitching like a hair-kissing Vladislav Delay on ‘1.3’. The smeared chords and scudding subs of ‘2.1’ call to mind Second Woman emulating the illusive dub-soul of False Aralia drops, and ‘2.3’ feels like distant rig heard on a Nitrous-induced permo. 

Sheer class for harder to please future dub freaks.

Edgar puts his kinky, Latinate stamp on myriad styles of Hi-NRG, gothic synth-pop, and cumbia, including a cover of Amanda Lear’s ‘Follow Me’ among its bevy of sleazy darkroom snax...

"Edgar debuts on Dark Entries with Pavor, an 11 track LP of sleazy disco, warped synthpop, and gothic cumbia. Veteran musician Luis Gutierrez has spent the past two decades touring in bands, running Lalalandia Studio, and building his practice in Oakland and Guadalajara. But now, for his first solo outing, he has become Edgar, a pop star who knows no limits! “Edgar feels mightier than anyone but is always reduced to his vices” says Gutierrez, and Pavor delivers vices in spades.

From the opening salvos of “Otra Agua,” it’s clear we’re in for a wild ride: seasick synths slide along slamming disco beats, menacingly chanted vocals sit amid a flurry of careening horror movie samples. The mischief does not abate as we’re guided through a demented funhouse of genre detournements. Edgar puts his indelible fingerprints over every inch of this vinyl, from uptempo numbers like the spooky chip-tune frenzy of “Nunca Mas” to the twisted cumbia of “Panteon.” We’re even treated to a fairly faithful (and majestic) Spanish-language cover of Amanda Lear’s “Follow Me,” here titled “Sigueme.” EBM, space disco, and horror movie soundtracks all find their way into the mix on Pavor, but the diverse palette comes together perfectly, like a Yello album for the 21st century.

On Pavor, Edgar brings us a healthy dose of pure excess, reminding us that dread can be a hell of a lot of fun. "

items.body:
reMASTERed edition of all 5 voulmes of Carsten Nicolai aka Alva Noto’s classic Xerrox series - exploring what happens when copies are made of copies of copies of copies etc..... a beautiful way to parse affective signals from noise and a big RIYL Ryuichi Sakamoto, Fennesz, Romance.

‘Xerrox’ marked a pivotal juncture of Alva Noto’s process-based, multimedia art, when it transformed from precision-tooled, pulsating minimalism to diffuse states of cinematic atmosphere. By the point of the first volume's release, Carsten Nicolai had spent over a decade rising to acclaim for his exquisite, minimalist glitch works, including contemporary classics in duo with Ryuichi Sakamoto. 

But ‘Xerrox’ would radically alter his work’s aesthetic away from microscopic, pointillist grammar to explorations of lusher textural and widescreen fascinations, systematically sampling and displacing familiar, everyday sounds - advert jingles, phone “hold” tones, film scores - within swelling symphonic structures that exist in paradoxical states of glacial stasis and noisy chaos, synthetic and organic, arguably sowing seeds for his work accompanying the lavish cinematography of ‘The Revenant’ years later.

The albums still hold an uncannily nostalgic pull over anyone who was there at the time, as Nicolai appeared to draw from his collaborator Sakamoto’s feel for misty-eyed melancholy across the set, resulting in pieces that feel like peak Fennesz in ‘Haloid Xerrox Copy 111’, or surely resemble pre-echoes of Romance’s swooning silhouettes in ‘Haloid Xerrox Copy 3 (Paris)’, or Michael Mann-esque modern city panoramas in ‘Haloid v Copy 11’, thru the Kevin Drumm-meets-John Carpenter tension of ‘Haloid Xerrox Copy 9’.

items.body:
Aftershock: The Seismic Impact of Dubstep, by seasoned music writer Lauren Martin.

"At the cusp of a new millennium, British electronic music was rapidly changing. Jungle and garage had broken into the mainstream, but were running out of creative gas – what fresh movement would next captivate the underground? On the outer edges of London, a small group of bass lovers had the answer. Through a new strain of subloaded beats that stripped jungle, rave, techno and garage for parts, this scene returned to the dub roots, prizing the fundamentals of soundsystem culture: bass, space and togetherness. They called it dubstep.

In Aftershock: The Seismic Impact of Dubstep, Lauren Martin charts the origins of one of the 21st century’s most innovative music genres in an oral history format. Through the testimonies of its architects and an immersive array of photography, flyers and unseen scene history, Aftershock chronicles the rise of artists like Skream, Mala, Coki, Loefah, Horsepower Productions and Rusko, as well as labels and parties such as Hyperdub, Tempa, DMZ, FWD>> and Skull Disco.

Together, this movement shook the British underground, exploded onto the internet and, within a decade, had rocked global music at unprecedented scale. Through first-hand storytelling, Aftershock is a testament to how the imagination and persistence of a few can transform culture."

items.body:
Stellar new album from Dave Sumner’s Function - arguably a sequel or sibling work to Sandwell District’s seminal ‘Feed Forward’ classic - marking his first solo LP since 2013, and best in his catalogue.

Running to 17 songs and nearly 2 hours of material, ‘Existenz’ works away from puristic, kick drum-led club tools and instead limns a sort of autobiographical story of Sumner’s relationship to techno and electronic music, all framed around a Videodrome-styled (David Cronenberg also directed the album’s 1999 namesake film) kind of occult cable TV aesthetic and strong nods to his early love of ‘80s electro.

Recorded 2016-2019, ‘Existenz’ is bound to surprise anyone who thought he just made heavy club tracks, and may well highlight his role in Sandwell District’s ‘Feed Forward’ album, which is arguably the strongest comparison in terms of their shared tone of mood, diversity of texture and structure, and, ultimately, their mesmerising effect. 

In total control of his sound, Function lures us into a labyrinthine, noirish sort of electronic thriller that embarks with the nostalgic Vangelis nods of ‘Sagittarius A (Right Ascension)’ and ends up drifting away in deeply romantic technohouse style with ‘Downtown 161’. What happens in between is primed for long headphone journeys and daily commutes, as the album weaves from spellbinding electro recalling E.R.P. to lush slow house featuring Robert Owens, to proper sci-fi electronic drones, samples of The Conet Project, and even breakbeat rollers, all interwoven with his signature acid and techno ligament and shine-eyed techno spirit.

"Composed between 2023 and 2025 after Jurg Frey withdrew from clarinet performance, this 54-minute chamber work places Heather Roche's clarinet within the string quartet of Mira Benjamin, Chihiro Ono, Bridget Carey and Anton Lukoszevieze, as Apartment House reveal a quietly extraordinary balance of stillness and motion, warm tonal color, intimate dialogue and a slow, organic passage toward unexpected transformation."

Finnish multi-instrumentalist Simo Hakalisto makes mosaic music of strings, bowls, bells, reeds, wind, water, and obscure electronics, threaded in subtle currents of color and texture. The title of his latest, Toinen Luonto (Finnish for “second nature”), alludes equally to Shakali’s earthen, tactile soundworld and Hakalisto’s deepening comfort with his craft.

"The album’s eight songs feel coaxed as much as composed, a web of resonances set in motion and allowed to simmer, build, or billow. Vibrations and silences unspool and intertwine, alternately pointillist and diffuse, attuned to some hidden harmony of the spheres.

In addition to his own repertoire of rare instruments (including a 36-string kantele, built by Hakalisto’s grand-uncle), several notable collaborators contributed to Toinen Luonto: saxophonist Julian Overall; Hakalisto’s partner in the duo Lunar Horns, Timo Juntunen, playing udu and percussion; American experimentalist Roy Werner; and Belgian ambient flute samplist Les Halles."

items.body:
Squid guitarist Anton Pearson takes a deep dive into kosmische waters on his solo debut, stacking elongated guitar drones, synth textures and organ vamps into billowing, free-flowing long form compositions.

It's pretty obvious how this one came about - the title gives it away immediately. While Pearson was touring incessantly with Warp-signed post-punk outfit Squid, his mind wandered incessantly, dreaming of a sound that Squid couldn't match up to. It haunted him, in fact, until he was back in his Brighton studio and able to experiment with the tools that surrounded him, not just guitars but synths and vintage keyboards. Thinking about the hallucinatory touring experience, music began to materialise that felt just as surreal, mundane and faintly entrancing. And it's a feeling that's best represented on the epic side-long opener, 'Driving Past the Muscular Cows in Belgium'. A good half of the duration is spent fixating on a restless drone that fidgets and buzzes like a car engine, retreating occasionally when Pearson's guitar mimics oncoming traffic. And in the second half, the low-end rumble falls away and the track begins to lift itself to the clouds, fading in vanishing synth arpeggios that form a bewitching final act conclusion. It's unexpected stuff, more like early Emeralds than anything Squid have ever stamped their logo on.

After the Fennesz-like granulations of 'Builder in a Bottle', Pearson hits firmer landscape with 'Tintinnabulation I', the first of two bell studies that lend the album some conceptual weight. Pearson admits that his debut came about through studio experimentation, which can often result in sketchy ideas that don't quite hang together. But 'Driving...' plays like a single thought and the two 'Tintinnabulation' tracks shine a light on the sonic space Pearson was immersed in. The titular chimes come in various formulations, smeared into shrill waves at the beginning before they're echoed by tense electric and acoustic piano phrases. And on the second, seven-minute section, the chimes are subsumed by thick, syrupy drones that increase in density until we're left with a spectrum-filling wall of synthesised sound.

items.body:
Recorded in 1991, 'Rise' sweeps up all known recorded material from A.R. Kane's Rudy Tambala and Cranes vocalist Alison Shaw, aka inrain, compiling a classic 7” for Rough Trade with additional, previously unreleased tracks. It’ll no doubt provide many with a first introduction to a prescient project by two scene legends, delving into shoegaze, dub, electro and trip-hop refractions of the highest order. It's the most essential Music From Memory release in a hot minute, crucial listening for all A.R Kane obsessives (that should be all of you) or anyone into Seefeel, Locust, Zurich.

For someone for whom Cranes' ‘Tomorrow's Tears’ and A.R Kane’s ‘Lolita’ are two absolute foundational texts, this reissue is basically something like a holy grail. Back in 1991, inrain appeared on Rough Trade's Singles Club series with a brief but brilliant 7" that sounded as if it'd been beamed in from another planet. A.R. Kane had already broken the mold, but these three tracks juxtaposed Shaw's dreamy vocals with dubby, spacious electronics and shimmering guitars in a way that wouldn't really rise to prominence until years later. Music From Memory do the heavy lifting here, remastering that original 7" from the original DAT tapes and adding the extra track 'Biology' and an alternate version of 'Sleep' to bump up the package. 

It's those original tracks that have us by the throat - we really can't believe they've been so slept on over the years. '...And Julie Rose' sounds like it should have been picked up for a Duophonic release a decade later, while 'Sleep' completely pre-empts Seefeel's 'More Like Space EP' that wouldn't appear for another couple of years. 

Prophetic, brilliant stuff.

items.body:
Mannequin tap an arsenal of secret German electro weapons, as played by Helena Hauff and I-F, hailing a pivotal era when body music set the scene for electroclash, stuffed with zingers FFO Le Syndicat Electronique, I-F, Dopplereffekt, Drexciya, Legowelt, Adult., The Hacker, DMX Krew, Gesloten Cirkel, and early Bunker Records electro 

“Active around the turn of the millennium, both projects share the involvement of producer Ive Müller while developing distinct collaborations and approaches to electronic music. H.E.I.M. Elektronik was founded in 1996 by Holger Erlenwein and Ive Müller (after the two artists split in 1999, Müller continued using the name), while MAS 2008 is the project of Ive Müller together with René Kirchner. Though separate entities, the two projects explored a similar sonic territory: stripped-down electro, minimal electronics and machine-driven body music shaped by analog hardware and a raw DIY production ethos.

The roots of Müller’s work go back to the final years of the DDR. As a teenager he worked as a licensed DJ — officially known as a “Schallplattenunterhalter” — operating a travelling disco across Saxony. With limited access to official Western releases, music circulated through cassette recordings taped from West German radio stations such as RIAS Berlin, NDR2 and Bayern3. Together with friends he travelled between youth clubs and discos around Leipzig with a “rolling discotheque”: a Russian Wolga pulling a trailer loaded with Electro-Voice sound systems sourced through the black market.

At the turn of the 2000s this background in underground electronic culture resurfaced in a series of recordings rooted in electro, EBM and minimal machine music. The tracks collected on Electronic Corporation 2000–2002 capture this moment: cold sequences, driving rhythms and stark synthetic textures produced with a direct and uncompromising approach.

Compiled and remastered by Rude 66 from the original sources, Electronic Corporation 2000–2002 documents a small but fascinating chapter of German underground electronics from the early digital era.”

items.body:
Modular bod M. Geddes Gengras gets the band back together on 'Guestlist', roping in an estimable team of collaborators (including Christina Carter, WANDA GROUP, Greg Fox, Ben Chasny and Meg Duffy, among others) to recapture the lightning in a bottle energy of Chicago's early post-rock era, when sounds would criss-cross over each other relatively freely.

Despite technology being accessible, commonplace even, it's still relatively difficult to find the sweet spot between live instrumentation and electronics. Modular synthesis, that thrives on its self-contained, often unpredictable moments of serendipity, adds an even more problematic element. You can make it work, sure, but so much of what we like about modular music is that it doesn't feel as if it's been looped into structures that file down its sharp edges. Gengras sets himself a challenge here, working like a synthesist but also drawing on his experience playing in bands - he sees both sides, which gives him a head-start. And he's also got the good sense to think back to an era where the possibilities felt endless: the "early Pro Tools" era as James Toth writes in the accompanying notes, when bands like Tortoise and The Sea and Cake were looking at artists like Autechre and AFX and wondering what techniques they could integrate.

And 'Guest List' is undoubtedly Gengras' most ambitious record to date. There's more to it than personnel, too - proper songs, a far cry from the hazy new age-tinted synth jams that we heard on 'Expressed, I Noticed Silence' or the post-kosmische "ROMpler worship" of 'QUIK-MELT', appear in the dense tangle of instruments and expressions. While the 11-minute 'The List is Millions Long' initially seems to not-so-subtly reference Tortoise's 'Millions Now Living...' with its chiming guitars and motorik beat (supplied by Portland-based sound artist Colin Blanton, no less), it gets more complicated when Will Epstein's saxophone enters the frame. And that harmonic complexity remains when the track melts into 'Laplace/Montagne' and Gengras' synth belches are augmented by Chasny's golden shreds. Hell, there are even vocals on 'Seven Dials' provided by Austin's Cory Plump, who shouts listlessly over Gengras' sunny arpeggios, Fox's drums and Duffy's riffs.

Prepare yourself, 'Guest List' is not the M. Geddes Gengras you're likely to be expecting. There's even a spoken word intro to the album's brilliant finale '"The Weather"' from cult social media star and sometime genius WANDA GROUP. Proper good.

Necessary re-up of a near 50 year old Afrobeat ace led by Fela’s regular sax blower, featuring Fela on keys, in the pendulous ‘Low Profile’ and a rework of Afrobeat anthem ‘Se Rere’ future-proofed by its slink trot...

“After years touring the world as Fela’s baritone saxophonist, Animashaun stepped forward to lead the legendary Egypt 80 band following Tony Allen’s departure, remaining the group’s musical director until Fela’s death in 1997. He continued on subsequent tours with Seun Kuti until 2016. Lekan began recording his only solo project, Low Profile, in 1977. The album was composed and recorded across sessions at home in Nigeria and on tour with Fela, who both produced the recordings and added keyboards to the album’s title track.

‘Low Profile (Not For The Blacks)’ referenced a government campaign during the country’s 1970s oil boom: “It was inspired by a speech by Olusegun Obasanjo, Nigeria’s military Head of State, when he urged black people to keep a low profile about their wealth and not to behave in a vulgar, arrogant way,” explains Lekan. “I argued that low profile is not just for the blacks, as everyone is human, regardless of race.” On the flip side, the simmering Afrobeat anthem ‘Se Rere’ (which translates as ‘Do Right’) delivers Animashaun’s message of living with integrity: do right, and you will reap what you sow. The song later became the band’s opening number during Fela’s live performances both in Nigeria and internationally throughout the 1980s and ’90s.

Despite recording beginning almost two decades earlier, Low Profile did not receive an official release until 1995, when it finally surfaced on Fela’s Kalakuta label. One of only a handful of albums led by core members of Kuti’s band, Low Profile captures a pivotal moment in Afrobeat history. Over time, the original has become a rare and highly sought-after record, and this new reissue places the spotlight back on a modest but influential Nigerian legend.

Strut’s reissue features the complete original artwork, is fully remastered by The Carvery, and includes brand new liner notes by Lekan Animashaun himself.”

items.body:
Working his hi-BPM (bull)rushes into swampy environmental recordings, Richie Culver returns to Boro's Industrial Coast with his most impressionistic and substantial Quiet Husband set so far, short-circuiting distinctions between his visual and aural practices with keenly synaesthetic nous hugely advised to admirers of W92’s Omen Wapta, aspects of Chain Reaction’s Matrix, or even H-Fusion’s ‘Captured Entities’.

‘The Architecture of Perception’ examines the lived and structural correspondences between techno and painting, proposing that tracks in the club function as colours do in the studio. On 'Composition', Culver sketches out his rough blueprint; first playing rich, noisy nighttime sounds - chirping crickets, oozing liquids - before looping them behind knee-trembling 185BPM kicks and metallic clangs. It's music that seems to revel in its own contradictory nature: minimal maximalism; faster, grubbier and more provocative than you'd ever expect to hear in a club.

'Abstraction' dispenses with the rhythm altogether, concentrating on creeping and evocative jungle ambiance that lubricates the brain for 'Duration’, where Culver's concept snaps into gear with buzzing cybernetic calls and sonorous outdoor sounds that dissolve into undulating 4/4 thuds. It'd be daft to label it dub techno, but if you compare Culver's muckiest gear to Basic Channel's earliest, most saturated mixing desk experiments, there's a similar level of intentionality: an understanding of space and tonal colour that permeates the rippling drive of the music. And Culver never lets his breakneck dancefloor instincts take precedence over his blustery experiments. The momentum flips back and forth, darting from the dancefloor to the bathrooms to the darkroom, heading outside for a lungful of fresh air (or a cig) before taking an about turn and rummaging thru it all again.

items.body:
An advanced masterclass in Berlin beat science, ‘Wireless’ is the final and arguably strongest solo release by T++; aka Torsten Pröfrock, an artist with a long lineage of important releases under numrous aliases - Dynamo, Erosion,Log, Resilent, Traktor, Various Artists and more - a true pillar of Berlin's Techno legacy.

First issued by Honest Jon’s in 2010, the 2x12” features samples of singer and ndingidi-player Ssekinomu (originally found on the EMI archival dive ‘Bellyachers, Listen - Songs From East Africa, 1938-46’) reworked by Pröfrock into a volley of rambunctious but rudely disciplined club workouts some 75 years later. In many other hands, this could have been just another passable cut ’n splice edit, but T++ treats the material with a balance of reverence and raving license, highlighting an instinctive understanding of the original music's intent and purpose, and their deep rooted connection to modern fast rap and hardcore dance musics.

The four tracks amount to a contemporary classic in their field and also exist in a strong tradition of German artists ranging from Stockhausen to Can and Basic Channel whose music has crucially incorporated the fluid, rolling nature and spectra of African drumming patterns. However, it’s vital to point out that T++’s take on African drumming is also filtered thru a love of UK music - Jungle, D&B, garage, dubstep - meaning that his rhythms are properly underlined with syncopated, technoid basslines owing as much to Kingston, Jamaica as Brixton and Sheffield in the UK.

For anyone who had been intently listening to Pröfrock's output since his Traktor gems, thru his Dynamo aces, to early work with Monolake and his string of seminal T++ 12”s in the 2000’s, on its release in 2010 ‘Wireless’ quickly came to epitomise his approach to broken techno production at its most open-ended and inexorable. Between the itchy, sprung step of ‘Cropped’, the puckish darkside torque of ‘Anyi’, a voodoo communal in ‘Voice No Bodies’, and the reanimated spirits of ‘Dig’ you have some of the finest mutant techno ever cut to vinyl.

An absolute must-have for dancers and DJs.

items.body:
After the cataclysm of their Om debut, Al Cisneros & Chris Hakius come right down with its hypnotic follow-up, now returned to circulation on its 20th anniversary FFO Sleep, Earth, Popol Vuh.

‘Conference of the Birds’ (2006) had big boots to fill after Om’s immense 2005 debut ‘Variations on a Theme’, so they effectively slipped into a pair of sandals instead, feeling the sand between their toes on a pair of more desert oriented jams. Still squinting at durational horizons, they take all the time needed - up to and over 15 mins per side - to concentrate on more brooding strains of modal, psych-inflected stoner rock that works it magic more subtly. 

The hairy nads-out appeal of their previous side, and the grungier tone of their earlier, cult work as Sleep is swapped out for mantric, pentatonic riffs and sway that channel the blues via Ethiopian music, kosmiche and hard rock in ‘At Giza’, placing Cisneros’ monotonic vox higher in the mix over shimmering backdrop of hazed hi-hats and uncurling bassline yoked with a tongue-tip tension.

But fret not heavy riff fiends, for that all comes with ‘Flight of the Eagle’, which effectively picks up where ‘Variation…’ left off, locking hard into a mantric cycle where Hakius’ damn slow but tight offbeat shuffles and the feedback worship riffs hold an intensity that breaks upward half way and soars in tumbling gyres to the end.

items.body:
A rare window into Angolan musical culture. Guitarist Mário Rui Silva folds traditional Angolan and West African rhythms into European jazz forms, creating music that's subtle, beautiful and completely distinct. 

'Stories from Another Time' compiles music from three of Silva's 1980s albums, "Sung’Ali", "Tunapenda Afrika" and "Koizas dum Outru Tempu". Silva was a researcher and intellectual who was motivated to find the roots of Angolan culture in spite of its centuries-long struggle with colonization. Spurred on by Angolan musical legend Liceu Vieira Dias of traditional band Ngola Ritmos, Silva wanted to understand the politics and spiritualism behind Angolan music. Dias took traditional semba and kazukuta rhythms and infused them into contemporary music in the '40s and '50s, helping Angola to find national pride as the country struggled to assert itself after years of colonial rule.

Luanda-born Silva attempted to do similar with his music - and while it sounds aesthetically similar to Brazilian music of the 1970s, this was almost accidental. Silva was in fact attempting to move away from Portugese-centered culture and its tropical fetishism, and develop a sound that was purely Angolan. The music is hard to place, it sounds almost out of time, both ancient and surprisingly contemporary, with soft pop hooks underpinned by complex polyrhythms and chiming mbira. The fusion feels fluid and considered - there's no cynicism here at all, rather Silva approaches his sounds with a deft, open-hearted charm that rings from every word and lightly-picked note. Huge recommendation.

Belgian avant-pop outfit Sergeant return to STROOM with a second album and a new member. RIYL Milan W, Total Blue or Animal Collective.

Since 2023's self-titled debut album, movie bro Benjamin Cools and actor Ferre Marnef have invited a new artist into the fold. The project was initially conceived as a live band, so the additional personnel just allows Sergeant to spread their creative wings; 'Symbols' is a more complicated record than its predecessor, packed out with byzantine arrangement and layered compositions, but it's also tighter. There's a feeling that their influences - '80s DIY pop, krautrock and post-punk - have been more fluidly lashed together this time around and Marnef's voice sounds more assured bedded in his collaborators' woozy, sometimes spiky productions. 

If their last record was "DJ Shadow in reverse", made from collaged elements and half-songs, 'Symbols' is a suite of proper compositions that dissolve as they play out, with tempos fluctuating and components mutating and vaporizing as Marnef sings. It's pop music that's engineered with Martin Hannett's ear for wacked-out production - fans of Ariel Pink (before he went full fash) or Panda Bear's 'Person Pitch' should investigate without delay.
